title: In 9 AI-written HTML pages, nearly half the tokens were SVG
summary: In 9 HTML pages an agent wrote by hand, nearly half the tokens were SVG coordinates. answer-me-with-html has the agent write Markdown and a CLI render the page: 8x fewer output tokens, 2.6x faster, about 15% off the bill: https://github.com/QingYunA/answer-me-with-html
body_markdown:
Ask a coding agent for an HTML explainer and you wait while it writes the page by hand. The answer-me-with-html project measured where those tokens go. Across 9 hand-written pages averaging 4,893 tokens, 47% went to SVG coordinates and paths, 17% to HTML tags and 15% to CSS. Only 21% was the text you actually wanted to read.

The skill moves the other 79% out of the model. The agent writes a short Markdown draft, a CLI bundled with the skill turns it into a page, and the project reports that the page appears about 50 ms later.

## What the numbers say, and what they leave out

In the project's benchmark (3 topics, 3 runs each, medians, Claude Sonnet 5.5 on a plain Claude Code setup), asking for HTML directly took 4,893 output tokens and 31 seconds. With the skill it took 612 tokens and 12 seconds. That is about 8x fewer tokens written and 2.6x faster.

The part I trust most is the caveat right after it. The bill drops far less than the writing, about 15% in their test, because every turn still reads the system prompt, your question and the conversation, skill or no skill. So the main gain is the wait: 12 seconds instead of 31.

The token counts are saved in `bench/corpus/tokens.json`, so `node bench/corpus.mjs` gives the same numbers every time, and the pages themselves are a download.

## When you get a page and when you do not

You keep asking questions the normal way. The agent decides whether a page is worth it, and the project's examples show the split:

- "Explain the TCP three-way handshake" gets a sequence diagram, a state diagram and a flag table.
- "How are the modules in this repo organized?" gets a folder tree and a call graph.
- "Redis or Memcached?" gets a comparison table and then a verdict.
- "Plan the cache change" gets real code from your files, with open decisions shown as options you answer on the page.
- "How do I show hidden files with `ls`?" gets no page, just a one-line answer.

Pages land in `~/.answer-me-with-html/pages/`. Buttons on each page switch the theme, collect your reply, and copy the Markdown that produced it. The project recommends an always-on mode, one rule in your rules file, so the agent adds a page to every conclusion and not only the hard ones. I would try it without that rule first and see how often you want a page.

The same draft format can drive explainer videos. Ask for a 3Blue1Brown-style video and the agent adds one line of narration per beat. `am video` builds a player page where the diagram builds step by step and the camera follows whichever node is named in brackets. The voice is inside the page, so it plays offline, and you can export MP4 with ffmpeg or WebM without it. The agent only makes videos when you ask.

## How it compares

The authors draw their own line against two neighbours. Archify makes one interactive diagram from a JSON spec. GenUI plugins such as dsh-genui show components inside one chat app. This skill answers the whole question as one page, mixing text, tables, code and diagrams, in any agent that can run a shell command.

## Getting it running

You need Node.js 20 or newer, and there is no `npm install` step because the CLI is bundled. In Claude Code:

```
/plugin marketplace add QingYunA/answer-me-with-html
/plugin install answer-me-with-html@answer-me-with-html
```

For other agents, `npx skills add QingYunA/answer-me-with-html` asks which ones to install into. Then ask about the TCP handshake, the same page the agent-driven install in INSTALL.md uses to check the result, and compare it against what your agent gives you without the skill.
